cards.details: First Tirthankara, also known as Adinatha. Believed to have laid the foundation of human civilization. Mentioned in Rigveda, Vishnu Purana, and Bhagavata Purana.
The 19th Tirthankara. A highly debated figure where Shvetambaras view her as female (Princess Malli of Mithila) and Digambaras view him as male.
The 22nd Tirthankara. Believed to be a cousin of Lord Krishna (Yaduvanshi). Mentioned in the Rigveda alongside Rishabhadeva.
The 23rd Tirthankara. Historically recognized figure who lived 250 years before Mahavira. Born to King Ashvasena of Varanasi; preached 4 great vows.
The 24th and last Tirthankara. He organized the monastic system, added the fifth vow of Brahmacharya (Chastity), and popularized Jainism.

traps.title: UPSC Common Exam Traps
items: Trap: Thinking all 24 Tirthankaras are historically verified figures. Only the 23rd (Parshvanatha) and the 24th (Mahavira) are historically attested by modern historians. The first 22 are regarded as legendary.

Trap: Confusing the gender of Mallinatha. In Shvetambara tradition, Mallinatha is a female princess (Malli Devi). In Digambara tradition, Mallinatha is a male monk. UPSC may frame statements asserting that both sects agree on gender.

Trap: Mixing up Vedic mentions. Rigveda refers only to two Tirthankaras by name: Rishabhadeva (1st) and Arishtanemi (22nd). Do not assume Mahavira or Parshvanatha are mentioned in the Rigvedic Samhitas.

Trap: Confusing Tirthankara emblems. Emblems of the key figures are highly tested (Rishabhadeva = Bull, Neminatha = Conch, Parshvanatha = Serpent, Mahavira = Lion, Mallinatha = Water Jar). Make sure to memorize these matches.

Trap: Believing Tirthankaras are equivalent to Gods/creators. Jains reject the idea of a creator God. Tirthankaras are human beings who attained liberation (moksha) through intense self-discipline and became teachers.

items.question: Which Tirthankara is believed to be the cousin of Krishna, and what is his emblem?
items.answer: Arishtanemi (22nd Tirthankara), and his emblem is the Conch shell (Shankha). He belonged to the Yaduvansh dynasty.

items.question: Which two Tirthankaras are explicitly mentioned in the Rigveda?
items.answer: Rishabhadeva (1st Tirthankara, also known as Adinatha) and Arishtanemi (22nd Tirthankara).

items.question: Who was the father of the 23rd Tirthankara, Parshvanatha, and where did he rule?
items.answer: King Ashvasena, who ruled Varanasi (Kashi). Parshvanatha was a prince of Varanasi before renouncing the world.

items.question: Explain the sectarian difference regarding the 19th Tirthankara Mallinatha.
items.answer: Shvetambaras believe Mallinatha was a female princess named Malli Devi, while Digambaras reject this, stating all Tirthankaras must be male to attain liberation, thus viewing him as male.

items.question: Which Tirthankara is associated with the symbol of the Swastika, and which one with the Swastika-like Suparshva?
items.answer: The 7th Tirthankara, Suparshvanatha, has the Swastika as his emblem. (The 8th Tirthankara Chandraprabha is symbolized by the Crescent Moon).

deepDive.title: Tirthankaras of Jainism: History, Emblems, and Literature
deepDive.description: A comprehensive analysis of the 24 Jinas, their symbols, Rigvedic references, historical profiles, and structural legacy in Jainism.

sections.title: 1. The Concept of Tirthankara & Historical Reality
sections.content:
A Tirthankara (literally 'ford-maker' or 'passage-maker') is a human being who achieves spiritual liberation (moksha) through intense penance and then serves as a teacher of the Jain path (Dharma). They create a 'bridge' or 'ford' (Tirtha) across the ocean of cycles of birth and death (samsara) for others to cross.

According to Jain cosmology, time is infinite and divided into cycles of progress (Utsarpini) and decline (Avasarpini). In each half-cycle, 24 Tirthankaras are born. The current era is the decline cycle (Avasarpini), and Vardhamana Mahavira was the 24th and final Tirthankara of this cycle.

Historical Attestation

In modern historiography, the first 22 Tirthankaras are viewed as mythological or legendary figures whose traditional lifespans are too long to be historically validated. However, the last two are accepted as historical figures:

  • Parshvanatha (23rd): Lived around the 8th Century BCE. He was a prince of Kashi (Varanasi), born to King Ashvasena and Queen Vama. He renounced the world, attained enlightenment at Sammeta Shikhar (Parasnath Hill, Jharkhand), and taught the Chaturyama Dharma (four vows).
  • Vardhamana Mahavira (24th): Lived in the 6th-5th Century BCE (traditionally 540-468 BCE). He reformed the Jain order and added the 5th vow of Chastity.

sections.title: 3. Vedic References and Textual Sources
sections.content:
Jainism's antiquity is supported by external ancient scriptures. The most high-yield associations are:

  • Rigveda: Contains explicit references to the first Tirthankara, Rishabhadeva (also called Vrishabha), and the 22nd Tirthankara, Arishtanemi. Rishabhadeva is praised as a great spiritual figure.
  • Vishnu Purana & Bhagavata Purana: Rishabhadeva is described as an incarnation of Vishnu, who taught the path of ascetics. He is noted as the son of King Nabhi and Queen Marudevi.
  • Yajurveda: References the name of three Tirthankaras: Rishabhadeva, Ajitanatha, and Arishtanemi.
  • Kalpa Sutra (by Bhadrabahu): Composed in the 4th-3rd Century BCE. It is the primary Jain source containing detailed biographies of all the 24 Tirthankaras, particularly Rishabha, Nemi, Parshva, and Mahavira.

In Jain literature, the Tirthankaras are part of the 63 illustrious figures known as **Shalakapurushas** (great personalities) who define the course of cosmic history.

sections.title: 4. Comparative Highlights: Parshvanatha vs. Mahavira
sections.content:
UPSC often contrasts the teachings and structures of the two historical Tirthankaras. Memorize this comparison table:

DimensionParshvanatha (23rd)Mahavira (24th)
Time Periodc. 8th Century BCE (250 years before Mahavira)c. 6th-5th Century BCE
OriginPrince of Varanasi (Kashi)Prince of Kundagrama (Vaishali)
System of VowsChaturyama Dharma (4 Vows: Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya, Aparigraha)Pancha Mahavrata (Added 5th vow: Brahmacharya/Chastity)
Monastic AttireAllowed monks to wear a simple white garment (sacelaka)Advocated complete nudity (acelaka) for absolute detachment
SymbolSerpent (Sarpa)Lion (Simha)
